analysis.title: Construction Spending Fell in September on a 5% Contraction in Residential
key_insights: Total U.S. construction spending fell 1.9% in September from August to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of $2.186 trillion, per the Census Bureau. August was revised up to $2.227 trillion from $2.203 trillion and was an 11-month high.
Total construction spending was down 2.7% year over year in September. It declined in five of the first nine months of 2026 and rose in only two, leaving a downward trend from the early-2025 peak.

Residential construction fell 5.4% in September and was the main drag. A pullback in home improvement after an August surge drove most of the monthly decline. Single-family was essentially unchanged on the month and down 2.4% y/y. Multifamily rose 0.1% m/m and fell 0.2% y/y.

Private nonresidential spending rose 1.1% m/m and 2.3% y/y. Office construction rose 5.5% m/m and almost 40% y/y, driven by data centers, which are classified under office. Excluding data centers, office spending was 8% lower y/y and down more than one-third from its pre-pandemic trend.

Private power construction rose 1.2% in September and is up more than 12% y/y. It has overtaken manufacturing as the largest private nonresidential category. Office construction is on track to overtake manufacturing as the second-largest category in the coming months.

Manufacturing construction fell 0.3% m/m and nearly 18% y/y. The pace of decline has moderated, reflecting normalization after the surge in federally supported semiconductor and clean-energy projects in 2023 and 2024.
Private nonresidential spending excluding the AI-related office and power categories remains weak, with softness in manufacturing, commercial, education and healthcare.

Public construction fell 0.1% m/m and rose 1.0% y/y. Highway and street spending, the largest public category, slipped 0.3% m/m and is up 3.5% y/y. Educational construction was flat and transportation-related spending rose modestly.

Less than half of the funding authorized under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act had been disbursed as of August, while roughly three-quarters had been obligated. PNC expects public construction, especially transportation, to keep rising over the next year.

PNC expects private nonresidential construction to post modest growth into 2027, with technology-related investment accounting for the majority of the expansion. Elevated input costs and energy market uncertainty, including Strait of Hormuz risks, should keep manufacturers cautious.

Residential homebuilding is expected to stay soft given weak consumer sentiment and poor affordability. The 30-year mortgage rate is near 7.2%. Support could come if rates fall below 6.5% or wage growth significantly boosts purchasing power.

sector_views.rationale: Weak consumer sentiment, poor affordability and mortgage rates near 7.2% will keep single-family construction under pressure.
AI-related infrastructure investment drives office and power construction and accounts for most expected private nonresidential growth into 2027.
Spending is nearly 18% below a year ago. Declines are moderating, but input costs and energy uncertainty keep manufacturers cautious.
Less than half of IIJA funds have been disbursed, so a large project pipeline remains.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Spending fell from an upwardly revised August 11-month high. The trend since the early-2025 peak is down.
Home improvement pulled back after an August surge. Single-family was flat and multifamily rose 0.1%.
Private nonresidential gains from AI-related categories offset flat public spending.
Growth is concentrated in data center office and power construction.
Roughly flat, with slight declines in highway and educational construction.
Rates have edged higher this year and weigh on single-family construction.

macro_indicators.indicator: Mortgage rate threshold for housing support
macro_indicators.interpretation: PNC says a fall below this level could support residential building.

risk_factors: Elevated input costs and global energy market uncertainty, including the Strait of Hormuz, may hold back manufacturing investment.
Persistently weak consumer sentiment and poor housing affordability continue to weigh on single-family construction.
Mortgage rates near 7.2% limit residential demand.
Private nonresidential construction outside AI-related office and power remains weak.
Growth depends heavily on data center investment, since office excluding data centers is down 8% y/y.
geopolitical: Uncertainty in global energy markets, including risks associated with the Strait of Hormuz, is likely to keep manufacturers cautious about new investment commitments.
